steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on an online strategy that lets a search agent explore a 2D area with obstacles by following a space-filling curve and evading obstacles on the go. Give background on space-filling curves, why they suit robotic exploration, what we propose, and the paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Origins of space-filling curves (SFCs) and their properties
- Applications of SFCs
- Robotic exploration and the coverage planning problem
- Why SFCs suit robotic exploration
- Our proposal: online obstacle evasion with an SFC
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Origins of SFCs and properties
  - 1878: George Cantor, interval I = [0, 1] mapped bijectively onto [0, 1] x [0, 1]
  - G. Peano: mapping also continuous and surjective; image in higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}) = Space-Filling Curve (SFC)
  - more SFCs: E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, G. Polya; see Fig 1
  - properties: self-similar (similar sub-curves); surjective map (passes through every point of \mathbb{R}^{n}); locality preserving (close points in I -> close points in \mathbb{R}^{n})
- Applications
  - data collection from sensor networks; ordering meshes of complex geometries
  - approximate TSP solution via Hilbert's SFC
  - Space Filling Tree for sampling-based path planning vs. RRTs
- Robotic exploration / CPP
  - one or more agents search/survey/gather info in a region, avoiding obstacles
  - sub-problem of Coverage Planning Problem (visit all points of region/volume)
  - CPP approaches: graph, grid, neural network, cellular decomposition; any can be used for exploration
- Why SFCs for exploration
  - complete and robust: time complete, robust to failure
  - extensible: dimension (2D -> 3D, similar grammar); number of agents (complete and robust with multiple agents); irregular area (Generalized SFC (GSFC) spans irregular quadrilaterals and triangles vs. square / isosceles right triangle)
  - non-uniform coverage: some parts searched more rigorously; Hilbert curve more time/energy efficient than lawnmower's path
- Our proposal
  - 2D area, multiple obstacles of arbitrary shape and size, explored using SFC
  - area tessellated (waypoints), cells connected in SFC order; tessellation with obstacle = unreachable
  - online strategy, evade obstacle on the go; modified waypoint when unreachable waypoint met
  - guarantees all waypoints reachable from initial waypoint are explored
  - works for all SFCs; Hilbert's curve used for demonstration
- Organization: six sections — II related work and need for new strategy; III SFC preliminaries; IV strategy, completeness, properties; V simulation results; VI conclusion, limitations, future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In 1878, George Cantor showed that an interval I = [0, 1] can be mapped bijectively onto [0, 1] x [0, 1]. After that G. Peano found one such mapping which is also continuous and surjective; the image of this mapping when it is parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}) is called a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). Later more SFCs were found by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, and G. Polya. See Fig 1. SFCs have some interesting properties -

- Self-Similar - Each curve is made of similar sub-curves
- Surjective Map - SFC passes through every point of \mathbb{R}^{n}
- Locality Preserving - Two points that are close in I map to points that are close in \mathbb{R}^{n}

Because of these properties SFCs have been used in a lot of applications - data collection from sensor network, ordering meshes of complex geometries and many more. Using Hilbert's Space Filling curve, an approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) can be found. Space Filling Trees, which are analogous to SFCs but have a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning, instead of traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs).

A major application of SFCs is robotic exploration. In the robotic exploration problem, one robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region and they have to avoid obstacles. Robotic exploration is a sub-problem of the larger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), where the agent has the task of visiting all the points in a given region or volume while avoiding obstacles. There are already many approaches for CPP - Graph based, Grid based, Neural-Network based, Cellular decomposition based. Each of them can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

- Why SFCs for exploration
  - complete and robust: time complete, robust to failure
  - extensible: dimension (2D -> 3D, similar grammar); number of agents; irregular area (GSFC: irregular quadrilaterals and triangles vs. square / isosceles right triangle)
  - non-uniform coverage; Hilbert curve more time/energy efficient than lawnmower's path
- Our proposal
  - 2D area, multiple obstacles of arbitrary shape and size; tessellated into waypoints, connected in SFC order; tessellation with obstacle unreachable
  - online strategy, modified waypoint for unreachable waypoints; all waypoints reachable from initial one explored
  - works for all SFCs, Hilbert's curve used for demonstration
- Organization: six sections (II related work, III preliminaries, IV strategy, V simulation, VI conclusion)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In 1878, George Cantor showed that an interval I = [0, 1] can be mapped bijectively onto [0, 1] x [0, 1]. After that G. Peano found one such mapping which is also continuous and surjective; the image of this mapping when it is parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}) is called a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). Later more SFCs were found by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, and G. Polya. See Fig 1. SFCs have some interesting properties -

- Self-Similar - Each curve is made of similar sub-curves
- Surjective Map - SFC passes through every point of \mathbb{R}^{n}
- Locality Preserving - Two points that are close in I map to points that are close in \mathbb{R}^{n}

Because of these properties SFCs have been used in a lot of applications - data collection from sensor network, ordering meshes of complex geometries and many more. Using Hilbert's Space Filling curve, an approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) can be found. Space Filling Trees, which are analogous to SFCs but have a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning, instead of traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs).

A major application of SFCs is robotic exploration. In the robotic exploration problem, one robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region and they have to avoid obstacles. Robotic exploration is a sub-problem of the larger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), where the agent has the task of visiting all the points in a given region or volume while avoiding obstacles. There are already many approaches for CPP - Graph based, Grid based, Neural-Network based, Cellular decomposition based. Each of them can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

SFCs have been used for robotic exploration and the reasons are:

- Complete and Robust: Coverage with SFCs is time complete and it is robust to failure
- Extensible: in dimension, in the number of search agents and in irregular area, as below
  - Dimension: A strategy made for 2D can be extended to 3D because similar grammar exists for constructing SFCs in both dimensions
  - Number of search agents: Coverage with SFCs has been shown to be complete and robust also when multiple agents are used
  - Irregular Area: The generalized version of SFCs, Generalized SFC (GSFC), can span irregular quadrilaterals and triangles, while SFCs map regular shapes like a square or an isosceles right triangle
- Non-Uniform coverage: SFCs can easily be used for non-uniform coverage where some parts have to be searched more rigorously than others. Also the Hilbert curve has been shown to be more efficient in time/energy than the lawnmower's path

We explore a 2D area with multiple obstacles of arbitrary shape and size using a SFC. The area is tessellated (the tiles are called waypoints) and the tiles/cells are connected in the order that the SFC gives. A tessellation with an obstacle is considered unreachable. We suggest an online strategy for a search agent to explore the area using the SFC and evade the obstacle on the go. When unreachable waypoints are encountered, the strategy suggests a modified waypoint. It guarantees that all the waypoints that are reachable from the initial waypoint get explored. The strategy works for all SFCs, but to demonstrate it we use Hilbert's curve in this paper.

The rest of the paper has six sections: Section II is about related work and why a new strategy is needed. Section III discusses preliminaries on SFCs. Section IV details the strategy, investigates its completeness and discusses its useful properties. Section V has the simulation results. Section VI concludes the paper and talks about limitations and possible future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In 1878, George Cantor demonstrated that an interval I=[0,1] can be mapped bijectively onto [0,1]\times[0,1]. Later, G. Peano discovered one such mapping that is also continuous and surjective; the image of such a mapping when parameterized in the interval I to higher dimensions (\mathbb{R}^{n}) is known as a Space-Filling Curve (SFC). More SFCs were later discovered by E. Moore, H. Lebesgue, W. Sierpinski, and G. Polya [1,2]. See Fig 1. SFCs have some interesting properties -

- Self-Similar - Each curve is made out of similar sub-curves
- Surjective Map - SFC passes through every point of \mathbb{R}^{n}
- Locality Preserving - Two points close by in I map to close by points in \mathbb{R}^{n}

Due to the above properties, SFCs have been used in many applications - data collection from sensor networks [3,4]; ordering meshes of complex geometries [2] and many more. An approximate solution to the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) can be found using Hilbert's Space Filling curve [5]. Space Filling Trees, analogous to SFCs but having a tree-like structure, have been proposed for sampling-based path planning [6], as opposed to traditional methods like Rapid-exploring Random Trees (RRTs) [7].

One of the major applications of SFCs is robotic exploration. In the robotic exploration problem, a single robotic agent or a group of them is deployed to search, survey or gather information about a specific region while avoiding obstacles. Robotic exploration is one of the sub-problems of the larger Coverage Planning Problem (CPP), wherein the agent is given the task of visiting all points in a given region or volume while avoiding obstacles [8,9,10]. Numerous approaches for CPP already exist - Graph based, Grid based, Neural-Network based, Cellular decomposition based [8]. Each of these approaches can be used for the robotic exploration problem.

SFCs have been used for robotic exploration, and the reasons making them eligible are:

- Complete and Robust: Coverage using SFCs is time complete and robust to failure [11]
- Extensible: – Dimension: extension from 2D to 3D [2] – Number of search agents: complete and robust with multiple agents [11] – Irregular Area: GSFC spans irregular quadrilaterals and triangles [2]
  - Dimension: The strategy developed for 2D can be extended to 3D since similar grammar exists for the construction of SFCs in both dimensions [2]
  - Number of search agents: Coverage using SFCs has been shown to be complete and robust when multiple agents are used [11]
  - Irregular Area: The generalized version of SFCs, aka Generalized SFC (GSFC), can span irregular quadrilaterals and triangles, as opposed to SFCs which map regular shapes like a square or an isosceles right triangle [2]
- Non-Uniform coverage: SFCs can be easily used in non-uniform coverage scenarios requiring some parts to be searched more rigorously than others. On top of that, the Hilbert curve has been shown to be more efficient in time/energy than the lawnmower's path [12]

A 2D area with multiple obstacles of arbitrary shape and size is explored using a SFC. The area is tessellated (the tiles are referred to as waypoints) and the tiles/cells are connected in the order determined by the SFC. A tessellation with an obstacle is considered unreachable. An online strategy is suggested for a search agent to explore the area using the SFC and evade the obstacle on the go. It suggests a modified waypoint when unreachable waypoints are encountered, and it guarantees that all the waypoints reachable from the initial waypoint are explored. The strategy works for all SFCs, but for the sake of demonstration Hilbert's curve is used in this paper.

The rest of this paper is organized into six sections: Section II elaborates on the related work and the need for a new strategy. Section III discusses preliminaries on SFCs. Section IV details the strategy, investigates its completeness and discusses its useful properties. Section V compiles the simulation results. Section VI concludes the paper and talks about the limitations and possible future work.
